description.narrative: The coffee value chain is under significant pressure. Persistently low and volatile coffee prices have made it difficult for many producers to earn a living income and invest in sustainable and climate-resilient farming practices. At the same time, gender inequality remains widespread within the coffee sector, while coffee production can cause environmental impacts such as deforestation, soil degradation and water pollution. Many of these social and environmental costs are not adequately addressed or reflected in the price of coffee.The Futureproof Coffee Uganda project aimed to contribute to a more sustainable, inclusive and resilient coffee sector by improving farmer incomes, productivity, soil and pest management, and the participation of women and youth. The project used a holistic approach that combined good agricultural practices, regenerative agriculture, income improvement and diversification, and gender and youth inclusion. In doing so, it addressed three systemic corporate social responsibility challenges in the coffee sector: underpayment, gender inequality and ecological degradation.The project brought together three Dutch coffee companies, three Ugandan value-chain partners and producer organisations. They worked closely with expert organisations and local non-gouvernmental organisations (NGOs) to implement activities in the coffee-growing regions of Zombo, Mubende and Ankole. A wider group of companies that have existing sourcing relationships in Uganda also followed the project and learned from its experiences. These lessons and results are used to inform future interventions and investments. In total, 4,120 farmers participated in the project, and approximately 2,400 hectares of farmland were brought under more sustainable agricultural practices. Gender inclusion activities reached approximately 2,000 farmers, women and households, while young people and youth groups participated in entrepreneurship and income-generating activities.The project’s regional reach included:• Zombo: 1,820 farmers, 862 households participating in gender-related training, and approximately 1,000 hectares of farmland.• Mubende: 550 farmers, all of whom participated in gender-related training, 82 young people, and approximately 800 hectares of farmland.• Ankole: 1,750 farmers, 665 women participating in training, two youth groups, and approximately 600 hectares of farmland.Over the course of the project, progress was made across all thematic areas. The most tangible results were achieved in the adoption of improved farming practices, productivity, income development and market engagement.Farmer incomeThe project contributed to increases in farmer income across all three regions. These improvements resulted from a combination of higher coffee prices, increased productivity and initial steps towards income diversification. The strongest and most measurable results were observed in Ankole. Farmers in Zombo benefited particularly from improved market conditions, while Mubende also showed promising income improvements, although these were less consistently quantified.Sustainable and regenerative agricultural practicesThe project made solid progress in introducing and scaling more sustainable agricultural practices. Farmers adopted regenerative approaches including composting, the production and application of organic inputs, improved soil management, better pest management and other improved farm management techniques.Early results indicate improved productivity, reduced pest pressure and strong harvest outcomes in several locations. Approximately 2,400 hectares of farmland are now involved in more sustainable production practices. Evidence of long-term improvements in soil health, climate resilience and sustained yields is still emerging. Inclusion of women and youthThe project made meaningful progress in strengthening the participation of women and youth in coffee production, household decision-making, entrepreneurship and additional income-generating activities.Women, men and households participated in training based on the Gender Action Learning System (GALS), which supports more inclusive household decision-making and the fairer distribution of responsibilities, resources and economic opportunities. Gender inclusion activities reached approximately 2,000 farmers, women and households across the three regions.Young people and youth groups were supported in developing business skills and alternative income-generating activities. Initiatives such as mushroom production and beekeeping created opportunities for entrepreneurship and income diversification, and several participating groups developed business models and generated their first revenues.Challenges related to production consistency, access to markets and the retention of participants will need to be addressed to sustain and scale the results. Overall resultsThe Futureproof Coffee Uganda project successfully laid the groundwork for a more sustainable and inclusive coffee sector in Uganda. It engaged 4,120 farmers, supported the adoption of more sustainable practices on approximately 2,400 hectares of farmland, contributed to initial income improvements and strengthened the participation of women and youth.The project also generated valuable lessons for coffee companies, producer organisations and other value-chain partners. It demonstrated the importance of combining agricultural training with market access, income diversification, gender inclusion and collaboration throughout the value chain. While some outcomes—particularly improvements in soil health, agroforestry, diversified incomes and youth entrepreneurship—will require more time and continued support, the project has taken important steps towards long-term and systemic change in the Ugandan coffee sector.
